claims.claim: Criminal defenses divide analytically into justifications, which assert that conduct the law normally forbids was permissible in the circumstances, and excuses, which concede wrongfulness but deny that this actor is blameworthy. Justification focuses on the offense; excuse focuses on the defendant.

A failure-of-proof defense is not an affirmative defense: it denies that the prosecution has established an element, whereas an affirmative defense raises new matter beyond a denial of the charge. Alibi is a denial of presence and therefore element-negating, though federal practice still requires pretrial notice of it on the government's written demand.

The prosecution must prove every element of the charged offense beyond a reasonable doubt, but a State may place on the defendant the burden of proving an affirmative defense by a preponderance of the evidence, provided the defense does not negate an element the State must prove. Patterson v. New York, 432 U.S. 197 (1977), upheld that allocation for extreme emotional disturbance, and Martin v. Ohio, 480 U.S. 228 (1987) (White, J., 5-4), upheld it for self-defense.

In federal prosecutions the defendant bears the burden of proving duress by a preponderance of the evidence. Dixon v. United States, 548 U.S. 1 (2006) (Stevens, J., 7-2), reached that result as a matter of congressional intent against the common-law background rather than as a constitutional command, and reiterated that duress, like necessity, does not negate the mens rea element of the offense.

Duress and necessity share a common limiting principle: if there was a reasonable legal alternative to violating the law, the defense fails. United States v. Bailey, 444 U.S. 394 (1980), stated that principle and, in the prison-escape context, required evidence of a bona fide effort to surrender once the coercive force ended.

Duress traditionally involves a human threat while necessity (choice of evils) involves pressure from circumstances or natural forces; Bailey traced this historical distinction and noted that modern cases have blurred it, citing Model Penal Code sections 2.09 and 3.02.

Jurisdictions split on whether a person must retreat before using deadly defensive force. New York Penal Law 35.15(2)(a) imposes a duty to retreat where the actor knows he can do so with complete personal safety, subject to exceptions including the actor's own dwelling when he is not the initial aggressor. Florida Statutes 776.012(2) provides that a person who is not engaged in criminal activity and is in a place he has a right to be has no duty to retreat and has the right to stand his ground.

The castle doctrine is a distinct rule about the home. California Penal Code section 198.5 creates a presumption that a resident who used deadly force against someone who unlawfully and forcibly entered the residence held a reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily injury, where the resident knew or had reason to believe the entry occurred and the intruder is not a member of the family or household.

Deadly force is generally not permitted to defend property alone; the Model Penal Code and most states do not authorize deadly force to protect property other than the home. Law-enforcement authority to use deadly force is constitutionally constrained: Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1 (1985), held that deadly force may not be used against an apparently unarmed, nondangerous fleeing suspect unless necessary to prevent escape and the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury.

American insanity standards come in several distinct formulations: the M'Naghten cognitive and moral incapacity prongs (M'Naghten's Case, 10 Cl. & Fin. 200, 8 Eng. Rep. 718); the volitional or irresistible-impulse test; the Model Penal Code substantial-capacity test, combining volitional incapacity with an expanded moral incapacity; and the Durham product test, which asks whether the conduct was the product of mental disease or defect.
New Hampshire is the only state that still uses the product test; the D.C. Circuit, which created it in Durham v. United States, 214 F.2d 862 (D.C. Cir. 1954), abandoned it in 1972.

The federal insanity defense was created by chapter IV of title II of Public Law 98-473, enacted October 12, 1984, which a statutory note records may be cited as the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984 and which also amended Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 12.2. Now codified at 18 U.S.C. 17, it is an affirmative defense requiring that the defendant, as a result of a severe mental disease or defect, was unable to appreciate the nature and quality or the wrongfulness of his acts; mental disease or defect is not otherwise a defense, and the defendant must prove insanity by clear and convincing evidence.

Kahler v. Kansas, 589 U.S. 271 (2020) (Kagan, J., 6-3, decided March 23, 2020), held that due process does not require a State to adopt an insanity test that turns on the defendant's ability to recognize that his crime was morally wrong. Kansas allows mental illness to show the defendant lacked the culpable mental state required as an element, and allows mental-illness evidence at sentencing, but recognizes no separate moral-incapacity acquittal.

Kansas is not alone: a footnote in the Kahler majority identifies four other states — Alaska, Idaho, Montana, and Utah — that similarly exonerate a mentally ill defendant only when he cannot understand the nature of his actions and so cannot form the requisite mens rea. Justice Breyer's dissent, with a state-by-state appendix, counted 45 states, the federal government, and the District of Columbia as retaining an insanity defense that inquires into blameworthiness.

An eight-state study by Callahan, Steadman, McGreevy, and Robbins found the insanity defense was raised in about one percent of all felony cases, and that only about 26 percent of those raising it were acquitted not guilty by reason of insanity. These are early-1990s figures from eight states, not a current national rate.

Voluntary intoxication is sharply limited as a defense. Montana v. Egelhoff, 518 U.S. 37 (1996) (Scalia, J., plurality; judgment 5-4, decided June 13, 1996), reversed a state-court holding that due process entitled a defendant to have the jury consider voluntary intoxication in determining the mental state element, noting the firmly established common-law rule that voluntary intoxication was neither an excuse nor a justification.

Infancy is a codified incapacity in some jurisdictions. California Penal Code section 26 lists among those incapable of committing crimes children under the age of 14 in the absence of clear proof that at the time of the act they knew its wrongfulness, and also lists persons who acted under an ignorance or mistake of fact disproving criminal intent, and (except for capital crimes) persons acting under threats or menaces.

Mistake of law is generally no defense, but the rule has narrow limits. Lambert v. California, 355 U.S. 225 (1957) (Douglas, J., 5-4, decided December 16, 1957), held that a felon-registration ordinance violated due process as applied to a person with no actual knowledge of the duty to register where no showing was made of the probability of such knowledge.

Where a statute makes willfulness an element, a good-faith misunderstanding of the law negates that element whether or not the belief is objectively reasonable. Cheek v. United States, 498 U.S. 192 (1991) (White, J., decided January 8, 1991), so held for the federal criminal tax statutes, while also holding that a defendant's belief that the tax laws are unconstitutional is irrelevant to willfulness and need not be heard by the jury.

Procedural bars can end a prosecution without any verdict on the merits. The general federal statute of limitations, 18 U.S.C. 3282, bars prosecution of most non-capital offenses unless the indictment is found or the information instituted within five years after the offense, except as otherwise expressly provided by law. Double jeopardy analysis for two statutory provisions arising from the same act uses the Blockburger same-elements test: whether each provision requires proof of a fact the other does not.

Raising certain defenses carries procedural obligations. Under Fed. R. Crim. P. 12.2, a federal defendant who intends to assert insanity must notify the government in writing within the time for filing pretrial motions, and a defendant who fails to do so cannot rely on an insanity defense.

The burden of production and the burden of persuasion are separate. The burden of production is the obligation to put enough evidence before the court to get the issue submitted at all; the burden of persuasion is the obligation to convince the factfinder to a stated standard. States vary: some require the defendant to carry both, others require the prosecution to disprove a defense once it is properly raised.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many states still recognize an insanity defense that inquires into blameworthiness, and how they group by test.
positions: The Kahler majority states in footnote 3 that four states besides Kansas — Alaska, Idaho, Montana, and Utah — exonerate only where mental illness prevented formation of the requisite mens rea.

Justice Breyer's dissent, with a statutory appendix, counts 45 states plus the federal government and the District of Columbia as retaining a blameworthiness inquiry, broken into 17 M'Naghten variants, 3 M'Naghten-plus-volitional, 10 moral incapacity alone, 13 plus D.C. using Model Penal Code variants, and New Hampshire alone using the product test.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two counts are consistent (5 mens-rea-only states plus 45 others equals 50), but the granular breakdown appears only in the dissent's appendix, not the opinion of the Court. The lesson states the five-state figure as the Court's and expressly attributes the breakdown to the dissent's survey, and notes the figures are as of 2020 and that legislatures change these statutes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Cheek makes a good-faith belief that the tax laws are unconstitutional a defense.
positions: A superficial reading treats Cheek as holding that any sincere belief negates willfulness.
The opinion distinguishes beliefs about what the Code requires from beliefs that the Code is invalid, holding the latter irrelevant to willfulness and properly withheld from the jury.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Verified against the syllabus and Part III of the opinion at 498 U.S. 204-207. The lesson states both halves of the holding. An automated summary of the PDF initially reported the opposite on this point and was corrected against the opinion text.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Dixon v. United States is a constitutional rule about duress burdens.
positions: Read broadly, Dixon assigns the duress burden to defendants generally.
The Court reasoned from the long-established common-law rule and what Congress is presumed to have intended for these firearms offenses.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Dixon as a federal, statute-interpreting result rather than a constitutional floor, and notes the opinion's observation that the federal circuits had divided on the allocation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often the insanity defense is raised and how often it succeeds.
positions: Folk figures and unsourced classroom numbers circulate widely.
The Callahan et al. eight-state study reports roughly one percent of felony cases and about a 26 percent success rate among those pleas.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the eight-state study by name, dates it, and describes it as eight-state early-1990s data rather than a current national statistic. No newer authoritative national rate was located by direct retrieval this session, so the lesson does not assert one.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive legal content about criminal defenses at all; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('Criminal Defenses is a foundational concept', 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'like reading a map legend') that asserted nothing verifiable and taught nothing about justification, excuse, or burdens.

The draft's vocabulary list defined 'Criminal Defenses' circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson', and padded the list with the generic terms 'context', 'evidence', and 'application'.
The draft's quickCheck items tested only generic study-skills propositions and had three options rather than four, with no source support, no difficulty, and no skill tag.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson with sourced content organized around the justification/excuse distinction.

Corrected an automated summary that reported Lambert v. California as 6-3; the reported lineup shows Douglas for the Court with Burton dissenting separately and Frankfurter dissenting joined by Harlan and Whittaker, i.e. 5-4.
Corrected an automated summary that attributed Martin v. Ohio to Justice Blackmun; the opinion was delivered by Justice White, with Blackmun joining only Parts I and III of Powell's dissent.
Corrected an automated summary that stated Cheek held a good-faith belief in the unconstitutionality of a tax law negates willfulness; the Court held the opposite on that point.
Framed Dixon as a construction of congressional intent rather than a due process holding about all duress burdens.
Attributed the state-by-state insanity-test tally to Justice Breyer's dissenting appendix rather than to the Court, and dated it to 2020.
Dated and geographically bounded the insanity-defense frequency figures instead of presenting them as a current national rate.
Added an explicit statement that the lesson is educational material about U.S. law, that state law varies, and that it is not legal advice.
